subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Calorie Labels and Food Choice
description: A fast breakdown of Calorie Labels and Food Choice for builders.

hook.text: New York required calorie labels on fast food menus. Average calories per order dropped by only 6%.

buildup.text: Calorie labeling gives consumers information. But information alone rarely changes behavior.

discovery.text: Traffic-light labels (red, amber, green) work better. Color coding triggers fast intuition.

twist.text: Labels help educated, health-conscious consumers most. Those at highest risk often ignore labels entirely.

climax.text: Effective food nudges change the environment, not the label. Smaller plates, healthier defaults, and repositioning work.

punchline.text: Information helps. But changing the environment helps more.

quiz.question: Why do traffic-light food labels work better than calorie numbers?
options: Color coding triggers faster intuition than numerical calculation
They were invented by more respected scientists

details.summary: Mandatory calorie labeling on menus and food packaging aims to help consumers make healthier choices by making nutritional information visible at the point of decision. Evidence shows modest effects, with reductions of 8 to 12 percent in calories ordered.
details.whyItMatters: Calorie labels are one of the most widespread behavioral policy interventions affecting millions daily. Their modest but measurable impact illustrates both the promise and limitations of information-based nudges for health behavior.
takeaways: Calorie labels reduce calories ordered by roughly 8 to 12 percent
Labels work better for informed, health-conscious consumers
Contextual cues like traffic-light labels outperform raw calorie numbers

faq.question: Do calorie labels actually change what people eat?
faq.answer: Modestly. Meta-analyses show an average reduction of 50 to 80 calories per meal when labels are present. The effect is strongest for health-motivated consumers and weakest for habitual purchases where labels are ignored.

faq.question: Why don't calorie labels work better than they do?
faq.answer: Most people lack the numeracy to interpret calorie numbers meaningfully. Is 450 calories for a sandwich a lot? Without context, raw numbers are hard to use. Traffic-light systems work better because they translate numbers into simple good-bad signals.
